tool.name: ReclassifyFeaturesInHSM
tool.summary: Assigns a fixed suitability score (0-100) to every cell of a habitat suitability model that falls inside your polygon features -- the standard fix for influences the base habitat factors could not capture: a new housing development still mapped as natural vegetation in an aging land-cover layer, a fenced right-of-way scored 0, restored land scored higher, a mapped disturbance footprint. Cells outside the polygons keep their original scores; NoData stays NoData. An active map selection on the polygon layer is honored. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Reclassify Features tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
Why this tool exists. Habitat factors such as land cover are usually built from remotely-sensed data several years old, so a habitat suitability model can happily depict newly developed land as optimal habitat, or recently restored land as unsuitable. The workshop book's remedy (section 2.6) is exactly what this tool does: digitize the unmapped influence as polygons, then reassign every HSM cell falling within them a new score that reflects your current understanding. Score a new subdivision or fenced right-of-way 0 (absolute non-habitat on the CorridorDesigner scale), a wildlife-friendly easement or restored parcel something higher. The workshop book adds a caution worth repeating: after tweaking a habitat map for a possible new development, a corridor model will still find a corridor -- the question is whether that corridor is any good, so evaluate it rather than assume.
What happens to each cell. A cell whose center falls inside any input polygon is assigned the new score (the same cell-center rule Esri's extraction tools use); every other cell keeps its original value, and NoData stays NoData -- the tool never invents data where the model had none, even under a polygon. The run messages report how many cells were reassigned, and warn if no cells fell inside the features (wrong layer, wrong extent, or an over-tight selection). True-curve polygons (geodatabase buffer circles, arcs) are densified automatically before rasterizing so they burn as full shapes, not as their few arc endpoints.
Selections are honored -- for map layers. If the polygon layer has an active selection in the map, only the selected features are burned in, and the run messages and output metadata record the count selected of the count total. This only works for a layer picked from the map: a dataset added via the Browse button is a bare catalog path with no concept of a selection and always contributes every feature. To reclassify only some features, load the layer, select there, then pick that layer here.
Run it again for different scores. One run applies one score to all its features. Different influences deserving different scores -- development at 0, an easement at 60 -- are separate runs, each feeding the previous output in as the next input. Each run's provenance chains cleanly (see below).
The output is the same model, modified -- and its record says so. The output carries the input HSM's own machine-readable analysis record forward with this modification appended as a post-processing step (feature class, score, selection note), the same model the corridor tools' Fill Corridor Holes uses: the output is the same analysis product, just modified, and the Corridor Analysis Data Report will describe the whole chain. An input with no record (an HSM made entirely outside this tool chain) gets a fresh record started here so the chain can pick it up from this point on.
Environments. This tool is grid-native: the analysis runs on, and the output is delivered on, the input raster's own grid and coordinate system. The Output Coordinate System, Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Mask environment settings are deliberately not applied -- honoring them would re-project, crop, or resample a finished analysis whose statistics and metadata describe the original grid. To get the result in another coordinate system, project the finished output with Project Raster as a deliberate step. The scratch workspace and overwrite-output settings are honored.
Credits and references. The original CorridorDesigner HSM tools are by Dan Majka (dan@corridordesign.org, 2006-2007); these ArcGIS Pro versions are by Jeff Jenness and Dan Majka. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org.

dialogReference.para: The habitat suitability model to modify, on the 0-100 scale -- an output of Create Habitat Suitability Model, Combine Habitat Factors, or Normalize Existing HSM. The output keeps this raster's grid exactly.

param.name: in_features
param.displayname: Polygon features to reclassify in the HSM

dialogReference.para: The polygons marking the unmapped influence -- digitize them right in the map if need be. An active selection on a map layer is honored (only the selected polygons are burned in); a dataset picked via Browse has no selection and uses every feature. Geodatabase buffer circles and other true-curve polygons are handled correctly (densified before rasterizing). Cells are tested by their centers.

param.name: new_score
param.displayname: New habitat suitability score for those cells (0-100)

dialogReference.para: The suitability score assigned to every HSM cell inside the polygons, on the CorridorDesigner scale:

bulletList.bullet_item: 0 = absolute non-habitat (a new development, a fenced right-of-way)
60 = lowest for consistent use and breeding
80 = lowest typically associated with successful breeding

dialogReference.para: One run applies one score; use separate runs for influences deserving different scores.

The modified habitat suitability model -- identical to the input outside the polygons. A name is suggested from the input; a path in a folder without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF. The input's analysis record is carried forward with this modification noted.

scriptExample.title: Reclassify Features in HSM example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Burns a digitized development footprint into an HSM at score 0, then scores a restoration parcel 60 in a second run chained on the first's output.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.ReclassifyFeaturesInHSM( r"C:\project\hsm\Badger_HSM.tif", r"C:\project\edits.gdb\new_development", 0, r"C:\project\hsm\HSM_Reclass_Badger_HSM.tif")
# Chain a second influence at a different score arcpy.jenness.ReclassifyFeaturesInHSM( r"C:\project\hsm\HSM_Reclass_Badger_HSM.tif", r"C:\project\edits.gdb\restored_parcel", 60, r"C:\project\hsm\Badger_HSM_final.tif")
